paragraphs: “Curiouser and curiouser!” cried Alice (she was so surprised that for a moment she completely forgot how to speak proper English). “Now I’m stretching out like the biggest telescope that ever was! Goodbye, feet!” (When she looked down, her feet seemed almost out of sight, they were getting so far away.) “Oh, my poor little feet, I wonder who will put your shoes and stockings on for you now, dears? I’m sure I won’t be able to! I’ll be much too far away to bother about you. You’ll have to manage as best you can. But I must be kind to them,” thought Alice, “or perhaps they won’t walk where I want to go! Let me see: I’ll give them a new pair of boots every Christmas.”
And she went on planning how she would manage it. “They’ll have to go by courier,” she thought. “And how funny it will seem, sending presents to your own feet! And how odd the address will look!
Alice’s Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender (with Alice’s love).
Oh dear, what nonsense I’m talking!”
Just then her head bumped against the ceiling of the hall. In fact she was now more than nine feet tall, and she immediately picked up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door.
Poor Alice! It was all she could do, lying down on one side, to look through into the garden with one eye. Getting through was more hopeless than ever. She sat down and began to cry again.

“You should be ashamed of yourself,” said Alice, “a big girl like you” (she might well say that), “crying like this! Stop this minute, I tell you!” But she went on anyway, shedding gallons of tears, until there was a large pool all around her, about four inches deep and reaching halfway down the hall.

After a while she heard the pattering of little feet in the distance, and she quickly dried her eyes to see what was coming. It was the White Rabbit, returning, splendidly dressed, with a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other. He came trotting along in a great hurry, muttering to himself, “Oh! The Duchess, the Duchess! Oh, won’t she be furious if I’ve kept her waiting!” Alice felt so desperate that she was ready to ask anyone for help, so when the Rabbit came near, she began in a low, timid voice, “Excuse me, sir—” The Rabbit jumped violently, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and scurried off into the darkness as fast as he could go.

Alice picked up the fan and gloves, and since the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself as she talked. “Dear, dear! How strange everything is today! And yesterday everything was just as usual. I wonder if I was changed in the night? Let me think: was I the same when I got up this morning? I almost think I remember feeling a little different. But if I’m not the same, the next question is, who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the big puzzle!” And she began thinking over all the children she knew who were her age, to see if she could have been turned into any of them.

“I’m sure I’m not Ada,” she said, “because her hair hangs in such long ringlets, and mine doesn’t curl at all. And I’m sure I can’t be Mabel, because I know all sorts of things, and she, oh! she knows hardly anything! Besides, she’s she, and I’m me, and—oh dear, how confusing it all is! I’ll see if I still know all the things I used to know. Let me see: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen, and four times seven is—oh dear! I’ll never get to twenty at this rate! Still, the multiplication table doesn’t matter. Let’s try geography. London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome, and Rome—no, that’s all wrong, I’m certain! I must have been changed into Mabel! I’ll try to recite ‘How Doth the Little—’” And she folded her hands in her lap as if she were doing lessons and began to repeat it, but her voice sounded hoarse and strange, and the words didn’t come out the way they used to:
“How doth the little crocodile Improve his shining tail, And pour the waters of the Nile On every golden scale!
“How cheerfully he seems to grin, How neatly spreads his claws, And welcomes little fishes in With gently smiling jaws!”

“I’m sure those aren’t the right words,” said poor Alice, and her eyes filled with tears again as she went on. “I must be Mabel after all, and I’ll have to go and live in that cramped little house, with hardly any toys to play with, and oh, so many lessons to learn! No, I’ve made up my mind. If I’m Mabel, I’ll stay down here! It’s no use their putting their heads down and saying, ‘Come up again, dear!’ I’ll just look up and say, ‘Who am I, then? Tell me that first, and then, if I like being that person, I’ll come up. If not, I’ll stay down here until I’m somebody else.’ But, oh dear!” cried Alice, bursting into tears, “I do wish they would put their heads down! I’m so tired of being all alone down here!”

As she said this she looked down at her hands and was surprised to see that she had put on one of the Rabbit’s little white kid gloves while she was talking. “How can I have done that?” she thought. “I must be getting small again.” She got up and went to the table to measure herself against it, and found that, as far as she could tell, she was now about two feet tall and still shrinking fast. She soon realized that the cause was the fan she was holding, and she dropped it quickly, just in time to avoid shrinking away to nothing.

“That was a narrow escape!” said Alice, quite frightened by the sudden change, but very glad to find herself still in existence. “And now for the garden!” And she ran as fast as she could back to the little door. But, alas, the little door was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table just as before. “And things are worse than ever,” thought the poor child, “because I’ve never been this small before, never! And I must say, it’s too bad!”

As she said these words her foot slipped, and a moment later, splash! She was up to her chin in salt water. Her first thought was that she had somehow fallen into the sea. “And in that case I can go home by train,” she said to herself. (Alice had been to the seaside once in her life, and had come to the general conclusion that wherever you go on the English coast, you find a number of changing huts in the sea, some children digging in the sand with wooden spades, then a row of boarding houses, and behind them a railway station.) However, she soon realized that she was in the pool of tears she had cried when she was nine feet tall.

“I wish I hadn’t cried so much!” said Alice, swimming around and trying to find her way out. “I suppose I’ll be punished for it now by being drowned in my own tears! That will be a strange thing, for sure! Still, everything is strange today.”

Just then she heard something splashing in the pool a little way off, and she swam closer to see what it was. At first she thought it must be a walrus or a hippopotamus, but then she remembered how small she was now, and she soon saw that it was only a mouse that had slipped in, like her.

“Would it be any use,” thought Alice, “to talk to this mouse? Everything is so out of the ordinary down here that I’d guess it can probably talk. At any rate, there’s no harm in trying.” So she began: “O Mouse, do you know the way out of this pool? I’m very tired of swimming around in here, O Mouse!” (Alice thought this must be the right way to speak to a mouse. She had never done it before, but she remembered seeing in her brother’s Latin grammar, “A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!”) The Mouse looked at her rather curiously and seemed to wink one of its little eyes, but it said nothing.

“Maybe it doesn’t understand English,” thought Alice. “I bet it’s a French mouse that came over with William the Conqueror.” (For all her knowledge of history, Alice had no clear idea how long ago anything had happened.) So she began again: “Où est ma chatte?” which was the first sentence in her French lesson book. The Mouse leapt suddenly out of the water and seemed to quiver all over with fright. “Oh, I beg your pardon!” cried Alice quickly, afraid she had hurt the poor animal’s feelings. “I completely forgot you don’t like cats.”
“Don’t like cats!” cried the Mouse in a shrill, furious voice. “Would you like cats if you were me?”

“Well, maybe not,” said Alice in a soothing tone. “Don’t be angry about it. And yet I wish I could show you our cat Dinah. I think you’d take a liking to cats if you could only see her. She’s such a dear, quiet thing,” Alice went on, half to herself, as she swam lazily around the pool, “and she sits purring so nicely by the fire, licking her paws and washing her face—and she’s so soft to hold—and she’s a wonderful mouser—oh, I beg your pardon!” cried Alice again, because this time the Mouse was bristling all over, and she felt sure it was truly offended. “We won’t talk about her anymore if you’d rather not.”

“We, indeed!” cried the Mouse, who was trembling down to the tip of his tail. “As if I would talk about such a subject! My family has always hated cats: nasty, low, vulgar things! Don’t let me hear that name again!”

“I won’t, truly!” said Alice, in a great hurry to change the subject. “Are you—are you fond—of—of dogs?” The Mouse didn’t answer, so Alice went on eagerly: “There’s such a nice little dog near our house that I’d love to show you! A little bright-eyed terrier, you know, with oh, such long curly brown hair! And it will fetch things when you throw them, and it sits up and begs for its dinner, and all sorts of things—I can’t remember half of them—and it belongs to a farmer, you know, and he says it’s so useful it’s worth a hundred pounds! He says it kills all the rats and—oh dear!” cried Alice sorrowfully. “I’m afraid I’ve offended it again!” For the Mouse was swimming away from her as hard as it could, stirring up quite a commotion in the pool as it went.

So she called softly after it, “Mouse dear! Do come back, and we won’t talk about cats or dogs either, if you don’t like them!” When the Mouse heard this, it turned around and swam slowly back to her. Its face was quite pale (with anger, Alice thought), and it said in a low, trembling voice, “Let’s get to the shore, and then I’ll tell you my story, and you’ll understand why I hate cats and dogs.”

It was high time to go, because the pool was getting quite crowded with the birds and animals that had fallen into it. There was a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet, and several other curious creatures. Alice led the way, and the whole party swam to the shore.
